subject: Science
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 45 minutes × 9 periods = 405 minutes
Total: 9 periods · 6h 45min

periods.stage_label: Observe and record the Moon's changing appearance
periods.activity_title: Tracking the Moon: What Changes Night to Night?
periods.activity_description: Students study a set of pre-drawn Moon-phase sketches spanning a full cycle, identify how the bright portion changes over successive nights, and record which shapes they recognise from personal experience. They arrange the sketches in sequence and label the waxing and waning halves of the cycle.

roles.role_description: Distributes the sketch set, prompts students to notice the direction and size of the bright portion, and guides sequencing without naming phases yet.
Arrange the Moon sketches in order, annotate which portion is bright, and record observations about how the shape changes across the cycle.

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens with the kite-festival scenario from the chapter — a student spots the Moon in daytime — and asks students what they already know about how the Moon looks on different nights.
Groups receive the sketch cards of Moon shapes, arrange them into a sequence, and annotate each sketch with a brief description of the bright portion's size and position.
Groups compare their sequences with neighbouring groups, discussing any disagreements about order and marking where the Moon seems brightest and darkest.
Teacher draws out the terms waxing and waning through questioning, without yet introducing the full phase vocabulary, and sets the stage for the next unit.

periods.teacher_notes: This opening unit grounds the chapter in direct perceptual experience before any explanation is offered — the goal is to surface what students already notice about the Moon, not to correct it yet. Watch for students who conflate the Moon being 'cut' or 'covered' with a physical object blocking it; this misconception will be addressed later when the chapter distinguishes phases from eclipses. A useful checkpoint: groups should be able to identify that the bright portion grows and shrinks in a repeating cycle before the unit closes.
materials: Pre-drawn Moon phase sketch cards (one set per group — 15 to 20 cards)

periods.stage_label: Observe and record the Moon's changing appearance
periods.activity_title: Naming the Shapes: Phase Vocabulary in Action
periods.activity_description: Students match the Moon sketches from the previous unit to the named phases — full Moon, gibbous, half, crescent, new Moon — and identify waxing versus waning within each shape category. They create a labelled phase-cycle diagram showing all named phases in order around a circular track.

roles.role_description: Introduces the formal phase names and the Indian terminology (Purnima, Amavasya, Shukla Paksha, Krishna Paksha) while students map names to the sketches they already sequenced.
Draw and label a personal phase-cycle diagram, placing each named phase in its correct position and indicating the direction of waxing and waning.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the formal phase names using a large reference diagram, connecting each to the sequenced sketches students built in the previous unit.
Students individually draw a circular Moon-phase diagram, placing all named phases in order, labelling waxing and waning arcs, and annotating Purnima and Amavasya positions.
Students compare diagrams in pairs, checking that the bright-portion direction is correctly shown for crescent and gibbous phases on both sides of the cycle.
Teacher consolidates by asking students to state one difference between a gibbous Moon and a crescent Moon, and one difference between waxing and waning gibbous.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit builds directly on the sequencing work of the previous unit — students now attach formal names to shapes they have already ordered, so the vocabulary has observational grounding. A common error to watch for is students treating 'crescent' as applying only to the waxing phase; make sure the diagram shows both waxing and waning crescents. Pairs who finish early can be asked to mark approximately where a half-circle waning Moon would appear in the sky at sunrise — this foreshadows the locating work in the next unit.

periods.stage_label: Classify and predict Moon visibility by phase and sky position
periods.activity_title: When and Where to Look: Predicting Moon Visibility
periods.activity_description: Students receive a data table of Moon phase, time of observation (sunrise/sunset), and sky position (close to Sun / overhead / opposite Sun), with some cells left blank. They use the chapter's locating rules to complete the table, then predict whether a given phase is best seen at sunrise or sunset.

roles.role_description: Introduces the locating rules — full Moon opposite the Sun, waning Moon visible at sunrise, waxing Moon at sunset — and demonstrates one completed table row before releasing students.
Complete the partially filled data table using the locating rules, then write a prediction for each phase about where to look and at what time of day.

time_bands.activity: Teacher explains the angular separation logic: on a full Moon day the Moon is nearly opposite the Sun, and as the bright portion shrinks during waning the Moon appears progressively closer to the Sun at sunrise.
Groups work through the data table, filling in sky-position and best-observation-time cells for each phase, consulting their phase diagrams from the previous unit as reference.
Groups share their completed tables with another group and identify any cells where they disagreed, then revise using reasoning rather than authority.
Teacher asks: why does a waning crescent Moon appear very close to the Sun at sunrise? — drawing out the link between angular separation and phase position.

periods.teacher_notes: Students are now moving from naming phases to classifying them by observable sky behaviour — a higher cognitive demand than the previous stage. A frequent confusion is reversing which phase is seen at sunrise versus sunset; anchor this by returning to the phase diagram from the previous unit and asking students to physically point in the directions of 'Sun' and 'Moon' for each phase. The closing question about angular separation is a deliberate probe: students who can answer it with reasoning rather than rule-recall are ready to move to the causal explanation unit.
materials: Partially completed Moon visibility data table (one per group)
Students' personal phase diagrams from the previous unit

periods.stage_label: Explain the causal mechanism of lunar phases and distinguish from eclipses
periods.activity_title: The Ball-and-Torch Model: Why Does the Moon Change Shape?
periods.activity_description: Students use Activity 11.2 from the chapter — a ball on a stick representing the Moon, a torch representing the Sun, and the student's own head representing Earth — to rotate through positions and observe how the illuminated portion of the ball changes, matching the phase sequence they have already named.

roles.role_description: Sets up the model conditions, demonstrates the starting position (torch opposite ball relative to observer = full Moon), and guides students to rotate systematically.
Take turns being the observer, rotating the ball through a full revolution and calling out the phase name matching each position of the illuminated hemisphere.

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the causal question arising from the previous unit: if the Moon's bright portion changes because its position relative to the Sun changes, what physical arrangement produces a full Moon versus a new Moon?

Groups run the ball-and-torch model, each student taking a turn as observer and rotating the ball through a full orbit while calling out phase names; one group member records which illuminated-hemisphere orientation corresponds to each named phase.

Teacher leads a whole-class discussion: what produces a lunar eclipse in this model, and why does it not happen every full Moon night? Students identify that the tilt of the Moon's orbit prevents alignment in most months.
Students individually write one sentence distinguishing how phases are caused from how a lunar eclipse is caused, using the model as evidence.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit addresses the central misconception flagged in the chapter — that Earth's shadow causes the Moon's phases — by letting students produce the phase sequence with the model before the eclipse distinction is introduced. Make sure the torch is the only light source in the space; ambient light weakens the contrast between the illuminated and dark hemispheres of the ball. The written sentence at the close is a quick individual checkpoint: a student who can write 'phases are caused by the changing view of the illuminated hemisphere, while eclipses occur when Earth's shadow falls on the Moon' has grasped the distinction this unit targets.
materials: White foam or rubber ball on a stick (one per group)
Torch or phone flashlight (one per group)
Darkened or dim area of the classroom

periods.stage_label: Derive the calendar units from periodic astronomical motions
periods.activity_title: Three Cycles, Three Units: How Calendars Were Born
periods.activity_description: Students examine the three nested astronomical cycles — Earth's daily rotation (solar day), the Moon's phase cycle (month), and Earth's annual revolution (solar year) — and construct a nested-cycle diagram showing how each cycle provides one calendar unit, using the chapter's Fig. 11.8 structure as a model.

roles.role_description: Presents the three cycles with their durations and explains why each cycle corresponds to a natural calendar unit, using Activity 11.3 (shadow-length tracking for the solar day) as a concrete anchor.
Construct a nested-cycle diagram labelling each cycle by its astronomical cause, its approximate duration, and the calendar unit it defines.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the solar day (24 hours, measured by shadow-length tracking as in Activity 11.3), the lunar month (approximately 29.5 days from the phase cycle), and the solar year (approximately 365.25 days from Earth's revolution and the season cycle).
Students draw a nested-cycle diagram — three concentric arcs or rings — labelling each ring with the cycle name, its astronomical cause, its approximate duration, and the calendar unit it defines.
Students annotate the diagram with one tension each cycle creates for calendar-making: the day does not divide evenly into the month, and the month does not divide evenly into the year.
Teacher draws attention to the mismatch: 12 lunar months of 29.5 days each give approximately 354 days, not 365 — and asks students to predict what problem this causes for a calendar.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit transitions from the Moon-focused explanation of earlier units to the broader calendar problem — make explicit to students that the phase cycle they modelled in the previous unit is precisely the astronomical event that gives rise to the month. A common source of confusion is students equating the calendar month (28–31 days) directly with the Moon's phase cycle; the closing mismatch discussion is designed to surface this. The nested-cycle diagram will serve as a conceptual anchor for the next two units on lunar, solar, and luni-solar calendars.
materials: Teacher display or blackboard for reference durations

periods.stage_label: Derive the calendar units from periodic astronomical motions
periods.activity_title: Lunar, Solar, Luni-Solar: Solving the Calendar Problem
periods.activity_description: Students compare three calendar strategies — purely lunar, purely solar, and luni-solar — by calculating the accumulated drift between a lunar year and a solar year over successive years, then evaluate how each calendar type addresses or fails to address the drift problem.

roles.role_description: Provides the key figures (354-day lunar year, 365-day solar year, 11-day annual shortfall) and guides students through the drift calculation before releasing groups to the evaluation task.

Calculate how many days of drift accumulate after two and three years, determine when the gap reaches approximately 30 days, and explain in writing how the intercalary month (Adhika Maasa) corrects this in luni-solar calendars.

time_bands.activity: Teacher recaps the 11-day mismatch from the previous unit and introduces the three calendar strategies: ignore the drift (lunar), count only the Sun (solar with leap year), or insert a correction month (luni-solar).

Groups calculate the accumulated drift at the end of year one, two, and three, identify after how many years the gap approaches a full month, and record how a Gregorian leap year corrects the 0.25-day annual surplus in the solar calendar.

Groups write a short evaluation of each calendar type: what it tracks accurately, what it fails to track, and which type best serves agricultural communities who need seasons to stay aligned with calendar months.

Teacher consolidates with the Indian National Calendar: a solar calendar following the Surya Siddhanta, established in 1956 on the recommendation of the Calendar Reform Committee chaired by Meghnad Saha.

periods.teacher_notes: Students are applying the drift arithmetic introduced in the previous unit to evaluate real calendar design choices — this is a step up in cognitive demand from constructing the diagram. Watch for groups who confuse the leap-year correction in the Gregorian calendar (adding one day every four years to account for 0.25-day annual surplus) with the intercalary-month insertion in luni-solar calendars (adding one month every two to three years to close an 11-day annual gap); these are different corrections to different problems. Groups that finish the calculation early can be asked to name one Indian festival that shifts date in the Gregorian calendar each year and explain why — this previews the next unit.
materials: Reference figures on board: 354-day lunar year, 365-day solar year, 365.25-day tropical year

periods.stage_label: Apply astronomical reasoning to explain festival dates and satellite observations
periods.activity_title: Why Does Diwali Move but Pongal Does Not?
periods.activity_description: Students receive a table of Indian festivals with their calendar basis (lunar, luni-solar, or solar sidereal) and their typical Gregorian date range. They classify each festival by its astronomical anchor, then explain — using their calendar knowledge — why luni-solar festivals shift by less than a month across years while purely lunar festivals can shift across different Gregorian months.

roles.role_description: Presents the festival table, reminds students of the three calendar types evaluated in the previous unit, and circulates during pair discussion to probe reasoning rather than recall.
First independently classify each festival and write a brief explanation for its date behaviour, then pair with a neighbour to compare classifications before sharing with the class.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the festival table (Diwali, Holi, Eid-ul-Fitr, Pongal, Makar Sankranti, Vaisakhi, Dussehra, Buddha Purnima) and asks students to silently note which ones they know and whether those dates feel fixed or shifting.

Students individually classify each festival by its calendar basis and write a one-sentence explanation for why its Gregorian date shifts or stays fixed, drawing on the calendar comparison from the previous two units.
Students pair up, compare their classifications and explanations, resolve any disagreements by re-examining the calendar logic, and produce a shared written explanation for the most contested case.
Pairs share the contested case with the class; teacher closes by connecting Makar Sankranti's slow drift (one day per 71 years) to the difference between the sidereal and tropical years.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit asks students to apply the calendar reasoning built across the previous two units to an unfamiliar classification task — the cognitive demand is now at the application-to-new-context level. A likely point of confusion is between luni-solar festivals (which shift but by less than a month, because the intercalary month corrects the drift) and purely lunar festivals like Eid (which can fall in any Gregorian month over a cycle of years); prompt pairs who conflate these to return to the drift calculation from the previous unit. The detail about Makar Sankranti drifting by one day per 71 years due to the sidereal–tropical year difference is a strong stretch question for groups that resolve the main table quickly.
materials: Students' calendar comparison notes from the previous two units

periods.stage_label: Apply astronomical reasoning to explain festival dates and satellite observations
periods.activity_title: Spotting Satellites: Artificial Moons and Their Orbits
periods.activity_description: Students examine a satellite pass prediction table (time, direction, brightness) and a list of ISRO missions, classify satellites by their purpose, and explain why satellites are visible only just before sunrise or after sunset — connecting their answer to what they know about reflected sunlight from the Moon-phase work in earlier units.

roles.role_description: Introduces artificial satellites as Earth's human-made moons, presents the satellite pass data and the ISRO mission list, and draws the connection back to reflected sunlight as the visibility mechanism.

Classify ISRO missions by purpose, interpret the pass-prediction table to determine which passes are visible, and construct an explanation for the sunrise/sunset visibility window using the reflected-light reasoning from the phase model.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the context of artificial satellites — orbital altitude of approximately 800 km, orbital period of roughly 100 minutes — and shows the satellite pass prediction table, explaining its columns.

Groups classify the ISRO missions (Cartosat, AstroSat, Chandrayaan series, Aditya L1, Mangalyaan, AzaadiSat) by purpose, then use the pass table to identify which listed passes occur in the visibility window and which do not.

Groups write an explanation for why satellites are only visible just before sunrise or after sunset: the satellite is in sunlight while the observer is in darkness, so reflected sunlight reaches the observer — an explicit analogy to how the Moon shines.
Teacher briefly introduces the space debris issue as a consequence of the large number of objects now in orbit, connecting it to the satellite classification students just completed.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit extends the reflected-sunlight reasoning students developed during the phase model into an entirely new context — artificial satellites — which is precisely the application-level demand the chapter's dissolution test targets. Watch for groups who describe satellites as 'emitting light'; redirect them to the Moon-phase model from an earlier unit and ask what the Moon and a satellite have in common as light sources. The reflected-light explanation written in this unit will be directly assessed in the final stage, so ensure every group produces a written version before the unit closes.
materials: Satellite pass prediction table (one per group — showing time, direction, visibility; can be a simplified hypothetical based on Activity 11.4)
ISRO mission list with brief descriptions

periods.stage_label: Trace each celestial phenomenon to its underlying orbital motion
periods.activity_title: Phenomena, Motions, Calendars: Closing the Arc
periods.activity_description: Students receive a set of scenario cards — each describing a celestial observation or calendar puzzle — and must trace each back to the specific orbital motion responsible, explaining the causal chain from motion to observable phenomenon to calendar consequence. Scenarios include phase prediction, eclipse conditions, calendar drift, festival date behaviour, and satellite visibility.

roles.role_description: Distributes scenario cards, sets the task of writing a causal chain for each, and circulates to probe the depth of orbital-motion reasoning rather than surface recall.
Work through each scenario card, writing a causal chain that names the orbital motion, describes the observable phenomenon it produces, and identifies the calendar or practical consequence.

time_bands.activity: Teacher frames the task: every phenomenon in this chapter — Moon phases, eclipses, the day, the month, the year, festival date shifts, and satellite visibility — can be traced to one or more of three orbital motions: Earth's rotation, the Moon's revolution around Earth, and Earth's revolution around the Sun.

Groups work through scenario cards (one card per group member initially, then compared within the group), writing a three-part causal chain: orbital motion → observable phenomenon → calendar or practical consequence.

Groups exchange one scenario card with another group and evaluate the received causal chain for completeness and accuracy, marking any step where the orbital motion was incorrectly named or the causal link was missing.

Teacher closes by tracing one scenario aloud as a model causal chain, drawing together the full arc of the chapter from the opening kite-festival Moon sighting to the orbital mechanics underlying everything students observed.

periods.teacher_notes: This final unit asks students to perform the exact cognitive operation named in the chapter's dissolution test — tracing celestial phenomena to the periodic orbital motions that produce them — across all four topic areas of the chapter simultaneously. A common slip at this stage is writing causal chains that name the phenomenon twice rather than identifying the orbital motion as the root cause; when you see this, prompt the group to ask 'what is the Earth or Moon doing?' before they write the first step. The peer-evaluation of exchanged scenario cards in the later bands is a deliberate accountability move: it surfaces gaps in reasoning that individual writing alone would not reveal.
materials: Scenario cards — one set per group (six to eight cards covering phases, eclipses, calendar drift, festival date behaviour, satellite visibility)
Blank paper for causal chain writing

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Observe and record the Moon's changing appearance
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students sequence pre-drawn Moon phase sketches, label the waxing and waning arcs, and construct a personal phase-cycle diagram with all named phases and Indian terminology in correct order.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can arrange the named phases of the Moon in correct cycle order, label waxing and waning arcs, and distinguish Purnima and Amavasya positions on a phase diagram.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Classify and predict Moon visibility by phase and sky position
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students complete a data table linking each Moon phase to its best observation time and sky position relative to the Sun, applying the chapter's locating rules to make predictions.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can classify each Moon phase by when and where it is best observed (sunrise or sunset, close to or opposite the Sun) and justify the classification using the angular separation between the Moon and Sun.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Explain the causal mechanism of lunar phases and distinguish from eclipses
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students run the ball-and-torch model to observe how the illuminated hemisphere of the Moon changes as it revolves around Earth, and write a sentence distinguishing phases from lunar eclipses.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can explain, using the reflected-light model, why the visible portion of the Moon changes as it revolves around Earth, and can distinguish this mechanism from a lunar eclipse caused by Earth's shadow.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Derive the calendar units from periodic astronomical motions
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students construct a nested-cycle diagram linking the solar day, lunar month, and solar year to their astronomical causes, then calculate accumulated lunar-solar drift and evaluate how lunar, solar, and luni-solar calendars each respond to the drift problem.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can identify the orbital motion responsible for each of the three fundamental calendar units, calculate the annual drift between lunar and solar years, and explain how each calendar type addresses or fails to address that drift.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Apply astronomical reasoning to explain festival dates and satellite observations
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students classify Indian festivals by their astronomical calendar basis and explain their date behaviour, then classify ISRO satellite missions by purpose and construct a reflected-light explanation for why satellites are visible only near sunrise and sunset.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can classify Indian festivals by their lunar, luni-solar, or solar basis and explain why their Gregorian dates shift or remain stable, and can apply the reflected-sunlight mechanism to explain satellite visibility windows.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Trace each celestial phenomenon to its underlying orbital motion
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students write causal chains for scenario cards spanning phases, eclipses, calendar drift, festival date behaviour, and satellite visibility, each chain naming the orbital motion, the observable phenomenon, and the calendar or practical consequence.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can trace each celestial phenomenon studied in the chapter — Moon phases, eclipses, calendar units, festival date patterns, and satellite visibility — to the specific periodic orbital motion of the Earth or Moon responsible for it.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and record the Moon's changing appearance
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can arrange the named phases of the Moon in correct cycle order, label waxing and waning arcs, and distinguish Purnima and Amavasya positions on a phase diagram.

competency.competency_text: Explains celestial phenomena including Moon phases, calendar structure, and artificial satellites by tracing each to the observable periodic motions of the Earth and Moon.

assessment_items.question_text: During the waxing phase of the Moon, which of the following correctly describes what happens to the bright portion of the Moon as seen from Earth?

options.label: A
options.text: The bright portion grows from a crescent toward a full circle.

options.label: B
options.text: The bright portion grows from a gibbous shape and disappears at new Moon.

options.label: C
options.text: The bright portion shrinks from a full circle toward invisibility.

options.label: D
options.text: The bright portion stays the same size but moves to the opposite side of the Moon's disc.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student has reversed the direction of the waxing and waning arcs — describing waning (Krishna Paksha) when asked about waxing (Shukla Paksha).
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student holds a misconception that the Moon's bright side shifts position without changing size, possibly confusing the Moon's orientation in the sky with the phase cycle.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student partially recalls the phase vocabulary but misidentifies the starting point of the waxing arc — gibbous comes after crescent in the waxing direction, not before.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the direction of waxing can be directed to their personal phase-cycle diagram and asked to trace a path from new Moon toward full Moon. Students who learned the Indian terminology (Shukla Paksha) first can use that as their entry point.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and record the Moon's changing appearance
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can arrange the named phases of the Moon in correct cycle order, label waxing and waning arcs, and distinguish Purnima and Amavasya positions on a phase diagram.

competency.competency_text: Explains celestial phenomena including Moon phases, calendar structure, and artificial satellites by tracing each to the observable periodic motions of the Earth and Moon.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Phase | Bright portion description | Paksha
Full Moon (Purnima) | Complete circle illuminated | —
Waning gibbous | More than half illuminated, shrinking | Krishna Paksha
Half circle (waning) | Exactly half illuminated | Krishna Paksha
Waning crescent | Less than half illuminated, shrinking | Krishna Paksha
New Moon (Amavasya) | Not visible | —
Waxing crescent | Less than half illuminated, growing | Shukla Paksha
Half circle (waxing) | Exactly half illuminated | Shukla Paksha
Waxing gibbous | More than half illuminated, growing | Shukla Paksha
assessment_items.question_text: Refer to the table provided, which shows Moon phases in cycle order. A student says: 'Amavasya and Purnima are both special phases because they mark the boundaries between Shukla Paksha and Krishna Paksha.' Is this statement accurate? Identify what is correct and what is imprecise about it.

options.label: A
options.text: The statement is fully accurate — Purnima ends Shukla Paksha and Amavasya ends Krishna Paksha.

options.label: B
options.text: The statement is inaccurate — only Amavasya is a boundary point; Purnima falls in the middle of Shukla Paksha.

options.label: C
options.text: The statement is inaccurate — Purnima and Amavasya are simply names for the full Moon and new Moon and have no special relationship to the two pakshas.

options.label: D
options.text: The statement is partially accurate — Purnima marks the transition from Shukla Paksha to Krishna Paksha, and Amavasya marks the transition from Krishna Paksha to Shukla Paksha, so both are boundary points.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student correctly identifies Purnima as a Shukla Paksha boundary but has the direction reversed — confusing which paksha each full or new Moon concludes or begins.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student has memorised Purnima and Amavasya as names without connecting them to the structural role they play as turning points in the waxing/waning cycle.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student has partially confused the position of Purnima in the cycle, perhaps placing it in the middle of the bright period rather than recognising it as the peak from which waning begins.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who can read the table sequence but are uncertain about the paksha boundary logic can be asked to point to where the bright portion is largest and smallest — those two points are Purnima and Amavasya respectively, and both mark the transition between the two pakshas.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify and predict Moon visibility by phase and sky position
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify each Moon phase by when and where it is best observed (sunrise or sunset, close to or opposite the Sun) and justify the classification using the angular separation between the Moon and Sun.

competency.competency_text: Explains celestial phenomena including Moon phases, calendar structure, and artificial satellites by tracing each to the observable periodic motions of the Earth and Moon.

assessment_items.question_text: A student goes outside at sunrise to look for the Moon. Which phase of the Moon is the student most likely to observe, and where in the sky relative to the Sun should they look?

options.label: A
options.text: A full Moon, directly opposite the Sun on the western horizon.

options.label: B
options.text: A waning crescent Moon, very close to the Sun in the eastern sky.

options.label: C
options.text: A waning gibbous Moon, overhead or in the western part of the sky, far from the Sun.

options.label: D
options.text: A waxing crescent Moon, close to the Sun in the western sky.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has confused waning with waxing — applying the sunrise observation rule but misidentifying which half of the cycle is visible at sunrise.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student correctly links the full Moon to being opposite the Sun but misapplies this to the sunrise context; the full Moon would already be setting in the west at sunrise, and this is a waning — not the most easily spotted — phase at that time.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student knows waning phases are seen at sunrise but misidentifies the specific phase that appears closest to the Sun at sunrise — confusing gibbous (far from Sun, earlier in the waning arc) with crescent (close to Sun, later in the waning arc).

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with sky direction can work from the phase diagram rather than compass directions — ask them to trace from full Moon backward through Krishna Paksha and identify which phase has the smallest angular separation from the Sun.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify and predict Moon visibility by phase and sky position
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify each Moon phase by when and where it is best observed (sunrise or sunset, close to or opposite the Sun) and justify the classification using the angular separation between the Moon and Sun.

assessment_items.question_text: Refer to the table provided. A student checks the calendar and finds today is day 11 of the lunar cycle (counting from the full Moon on day 1). Using the pattern in the table, predict the best time to observe the Moon today and describe approximately where in the sky it will appear relative to the Sun.

options.label: A
options.text: Best seen at midnight; the Moon will be opposite the Sun, almost fully illuminated.

options.label: B
options.text: Best seen at sunrise; the Moon will appear between overhead and very close to the Sun — a waning crescent low in the eastern sky.

options.label: C
options.text: Best seen at sunrise; the Moon will appear overhead, as a half-circle shape.

options.label: D
options.text: Best seen at sunset; the Moon will appear as a waxing crescent close to the Sun in the western sky.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has correctly interpolated between data points for observation time but assigned the wrong direction of the cycle — applying the waxing-crescent logic (sunset) instead of the waning-crescent logic (sunrise) for day 11.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student anchors to the full Moon rows (days 1 and 29) and incorrectly concludes that intermediate days still show a near-full Moon at midnight, missing the progressive change in angular separation.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student correctly identifies sunrise as the observation time but stops at the day-8 data point rather than interpolating to day 11, where the Moon has moved further along the waning arc toward the crescent.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find interpolation difficult can be encouraged to mark day 11 on a number line between day 8 and day 15 from the table and reason about which direction the angular separation is moving.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify and predict Moon visibility by phase and sky position
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify each Moon phase by when and where it is best observed (sunrise or sunset, close to or opposite the Sun) and justify the classification using the angular separation between the Moon and Sun.

competency.competency_text: Explains celestial phenomena including Moon phases, calendar structure, and artificial satellites by tracing each to the observable periodic motions of the Earth and Moon.

assessment_items.question_text: The Moon rises approximately 50 minutes later each day. Explain why this happens, using what you know about the Moon's motion relative to the Earth and the Earth's rotation.
expected_elements: The Moon moves forward in its orbit around Earth each day, so it is no longer in the same position when Earth completes one full rotation.
Earth must rotate a little further — approximately 50 minutes' worth — for the Moon to return to the same apparent position in the sky.
This means moonrise occurs progressively later each successive night.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who find pure verbal explanation difficult can be invited to draw a simple diagram showing Earth rotating and the Moon having moved along its orbit — the 50-minute delay emerges naturally from the geometry. Students who express this in terms of 'the Moon runs ahead of the Earth's spin' are demonstrating the same understanding through different language.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain the causal mechanism of lunar phases and distinguish from eclipses
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain, using the reflected-light model, why the visible portion of the Moon changes as it revolves around Earth, and can distinguish this mechanism from a lunar eclipse caused by Earth's shadow.

competency.competency_text: Explains celestial phenomena including Moon phases, calendar structure, and artificial satellites by tracing each to the observable periodic motions of the Earth and Moon.

assessment_items.question_text: In the ball-and-torch model, what does the ball represent, and what causes the observer to see different amounts of the bright half of the ball as the ball is rotated?

options.label: A
options.text: The ball represents the Earth; the observer sees different amounts of the bright half because the ball rotates on its own axis away from the torch.

options.label: B
options.text: The ball represents the Moon; the observer sees different amounts of the bright half because Earth's shadow progressively covers different portions of the ball.

options.label: C
options.text: The ball represents the Moon; the observer sees different amounts of the bright half because the Moon emits its own light on a cycle matching its revolution period.

options.label: D
options.text: The ball represents the Moon; the observer sees different amounts of the illuminated hemisphere because the ball's position relative to the observer and the torch changes as it revolves.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student holds the key misconception the chapter addresses — attributing phase changes to Earth's shadow rather than to the changing view of the illuminated hemisphere; this is the eclipse confusion.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student has misidentified which object in the model corresponds to which celestial body, swapping the Moon and Earth roles.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student has not grasped that the Moon reflects rather than emits light — a foundational misconception that would invalidate the entire reflected-light explanation.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who select the shadow option can be asked to re-run the model and check whether the observer's head (Earth) is ever between the torch (Sun) and the ball (Moon) during a normal phase cycle — they will find this happens only in a specific alignment, not continuously.

assessment_items.question_text: Lunar eclipses occur only on full Moon days, yet a lunar eclipse does not happen every full Moon night. Which of the following best explains why?

options.label: A
options.text: A lunar eclipse requires both the Moon and the Sun to be on the same side of Earth, which happens less frequently than a full Moon.

options.label: B
options.text: Earth's shadow is too small to cover the Moon except on special full Moon nights when the Moon is closest to Earth.

options.label: C
options.text: The Moon is too far from Earth at most full Moons for Earth's shadow to reach it.

options.label: D
options.text: The Moon's orbit is slightly tilted relative to Earth's orbit around the Sun, so the Sun, Earth, and Moon are not perfectly aligned at every full Moon.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student confuses the geometry of orbital tilt with variation in the Moon's orbital distance (apogee/perigee), introducing a concept not presented in this chapter as the explanatory factor.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student conflates the size of Earth's shadow with the orbital tilt issue — partially correct intuition (shadow geometry matters) but wrong causal factor; the chapter specifically cites orbital tilt.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student has the geometry of a lunar eclipse reversed — a lunar eclipse requires Earth between the Sun and Moon (full Moon alignment), not Sun and Moon on the same side, indicating a fundamental confusion about the eclipse geometry.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who select the distance or shadow-size option can be guided back to the ball-and-torch model and asked: what would have to change in the setup for the ball to pass through the observer's shadow at every full-orbit position?

assessment_items.question_text: A classmate says: 'During Krishna Paksha, the dark part of the Moon is caused by Earth's shadow slowly covering it.' Write a response that identifies what is wrong with this explanation and provides the correct cause.
expected_elements: The classmate's explanation incorrectly attributes the dark portion of the Moon to Earth's shadow — this is actually the cause of a lunar eclipse, not of the regular phase cycle.
The correct cause: the Moon shines by reflecting sunlight; the hemisphere facing the Sun is always illuminated, and the hemisphere facing away is always dark.

As the Moon revolves around Earth, the fraction of the illuminated hemisphere visible to an observer on Earth changes — during Krishna Paksha we see progressively less of the illuminated hemisphere, not because a shadow covers it but because the Moon's orbital position causes us to view more of the dark hemisphere.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who struggle to articulate the reflected-light mechanism in words can be directed to draw two diagrams side by side — one showing a full Moon position (illuminated hemisphere facing Earth) and one showing a new Moon position — and label what fraction of the bright side is visible in each. The written response can then describe the diagram.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can identify the orbital motion responsible for each of the three fundamental calendar units, calculate the annual drift between lunar and solar years, and explain how each calendar type addresses or fails to address that drift.

competency.competency_text: Explains celestial phenomena including Moon phases, calendar structure, and artificial satellites by tracing each to the observable periodic motions of the Earth and Moon.

assessment_items.question_text: Which astronomical motion provides the basis for the calendar unit called the month, and what is the approximate duration of one such cycle?

options.label: A
options.text: Earth's revolution around the Sun divided into 12 equal parts — approximately 30.4 days.

options.label: B
options.text: Earth's rotation on its axis — approximately 29.5 hours.

options.label: C
options.text: The Moon's phase cycle, driven by the Moon's revolution around Earth — approximately 29.5 days.

options.label: D
options.text: The Moon's revolution around Earth measured against the background stars (sidereal month) — approximately 27.3 days.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student has confused the astronomical motion that gives the month with the motion that gives the day — a category confusion between Earth's rotation (day) and the Moon's orbital period (month), with an incorrect unit.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student has reversed the direction of the derivation — dividing the solar year into 12 instead of deriving the month from the Moon's own phase cycle; this conflates the solar calendar's administrative month with the astronomical basis for the month.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has accessed a more precise astronomical fact (sidereal month of 27.3 days) but selected a quantity different from the observable phase cycle (synodic month of 29.5 days) that calendars actually use — showing detailed but misapplied recall.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who confuse the sidereal and synodic months can be reminded that the phase cycle is what is directly observable — the time from one full Moon to the next — and that calendar months are based on this observable cycle, not the background-star measurement.

assessment_items.stage_label: Derive the calendar units from periodic astronomical motions
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can identify the orbital motion responsible for each of the three fundamental calendar units, calculate the annual drift between lunar and solar years, and explain how each calendar type addresses or fails to address that drift.

assessment_items.question_text: A purely lunar calendar counts 12 months each of approximately 29.5 days, giving a lunar year of about 354 days. If a harvest festival is celebrated in month 7 of this lunar calendar, after how many years will the festival occur approximately one full month earlier in the seasons, and what does this illustrate about purely lunar calendars?

options.label: A
options.text: After about 11 years, because the annual shortfall of 1 day accumulates to a full month in that time; this illustrates that lunar calendars are nearly as accurate as solar calendars.

options.label: B
options.text: After about 12 years, because it takes one full orbit of the Moon around Earth for the drift to accumulate; this illustrates that the Moon's orbital period determines how quickly seasons shift.

options.label: C
options.text: After about 3 years, because the annual shortfall of approximately 11 days accumulates to a full month in that time; this illustrates that a purely lunar calendar gradually drifts out of alignment with the seasons.

options.label: D
options.text: After about 4 years, because the Gregorian leap year cycle of 4 years corrects the drift; this illustrates that lunar and solar calendars are kept synchronised by the same mechanism.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student has misremembered the annual shortfall as 1 day rather than 11 days, producing the wrong accumulation time and incorrectly concluding that lunar and solar calendars are nearly equivalent in accuracy.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student confuses the Gregorian leap-year correction (which addresses the 0.25-day annual surplus in the solar calendar) with the much larger lunar-solar drift problem — applying the wrong corrective mechanism to the wrong calendar.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student confuses the timescale of one Moon orbit (approximately one month) with the accumulation time for the annual lunar-solar shortfall to reach a full month, and incorrectly attributes the drift rate to the Moon's orbital period.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are uncertain about the calculation can be asked to write out year 1 (11 days short), year 2 (22 days short), year 3 (33 days short) and identify when the gap first exceeds 29.5 days — this makes the approximately 3-year accumulation concrete without requiring formula use.

assessment_items.stage_label: Derive the calendar units from periodic astronomical motions
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can identify the orbital motion responsible for each of the three fundamental calendar units, calculate the annual drift between lunar and solar years, and explain how each calendar type addresses or fails to address that drift.

assessment_items.question_text: The Gregorian calendar adds an extra day to February every four years. Explain what astronomical fact makes this necessary, and state one rule that prevents the leap year from being applied in certain century years.
expected_elements: Earth's revolution around the Sun takes approximately 365.25 days, not exactly 365 days — the extra 0.25 days per year accumulates to approximately one full day every four years.
Adding a 29th day to February every four years corrects this accumulation and keeps the calendar aligned with the solar year and the seasons.
Century years (e.g. 1700, 1800, 1900) skip the leap year because the 0.25-day estimate overcorrects slightly over a century; however, every 400th year (e.g. 1600, 2000) the leap year is restored.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who can state the leap-year rule without explaining the 0.25-day accumulation should be prompted with: 'Why does the quarter-day cause a problem — what would happen after 100 years without any correction?' Students who prefer numerical reasoning can be asked to calculate the total accumulated extra time after 100 years at 0.25 days per year and explain why a century correction is needed.

assessment_items.stage_label: Apply astronomical reasoning to explain festival dates and satellite observations
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify Indian festivals by their lunar, luni-solar, or solar basis and explain why their Gregorian dates shift or remain stable, and can apply the reflected-sunlight mechanism to explain satellite visibility windows.

assessment_items.question_text: Diwali is celebrated on the new Moon of the month of Kartika in the luni-solar calendar. Pongal is celebrated in the solar sidereal calendar on approximately the same Gregorian date each year. Which statement best explains why Diwali's Gregorian date shifts by up to a month across years while Pongal's date remains nearly fixed?

options.label: A
options.text: Diwali is tied to a lunar phase date that shifts relative to the solar year but is corrected by the intercalary month, keeping it within roughly a month's range; Pongal is tied directly to an event in Earth's solar orbit and therefore falls on nearly the same Gregorian date annually.

options.label: B
options.text: Diwali shifts because Indian luni-solar calendars count from the new Moon, while Pongal is fixed because the solar sidereal calendar counts from the full Moon.

options.label: C
options.text: Diwali shifts because it falls on the new Moon, which occurs on a different date each month; Pongal is fixed because it always falls on a full Moon date in the solar calendar.

options.label: D
options.text: Diwali shifts because luni-solar calendars do not use any correction for the lunar-solar drift; Pongal is fixed because the solar sidereal calendar uses a leap year identical to the Gregorian calendar.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student confuses the mechanism of Diwali's date shift (lunar-solar drift corrected by intercalary month) with simply the fact that new Moons fall on different dates — missing the structural calendar explanation — and incorrectly assigns Pongal to a full Moon.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student incorrectly states that luni-solar calendars have no correction for drift — directly contradicting the chapter's content about the intercalary month (Adhika Maasa) — and incorrectly equates the solar sidereal leap year with the Gregorian leap year.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student has replaced the calendar-type explanation with the Amant/Purnimant convention difference (new Moon vs. full Moon month-start), confusing an internal luni-solar calendar convention with the reason festivals have fixed or shifting Gregorian dates.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are uncertain about why luni-solar festivals shift by less than a month (rather than cycling freely like purely lunar festivals) can be directed back to the drift calculation from the previous stage: the intercalary month prevents the accumulated gap from ever exceeding roughly one full month.

assessment_items.question_text: Artificial satellites orbiting Earth at about 800 km altitude are visible to the naked eye only just before sunrise or just after sunset. What is the correct explanation for this visibility window?

options.label: A
options.text: The satellite emits a bright signal light that is only switched on at sunrise and sunset for energy-saving purposes.

options.label: B
options.text: The satellite is still in sunlight and reflecting sunlight toward the observer, while the observer on the ground is in darkness — the same reason the Moon is seen by reflected sunlight.

options.label: C
options.text: The satellite is visible only when it passes directly overhead, which occurs only at sunrise and sunset due to its orbital period of 100 minutes.

options.label: D
options.text: The satellite reflects light from the Moon rather than the Sun, and the Moon is brightest near the horizon at sunrise and sunset.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student has not applied the reflected-light mechanism at all and instead invents a technological explanation — indicating that the connection between Moon-phase reflected sunlight and satellite visibility was not made.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student confuses the satellite's orbital geometry (when it passes overhead) with the lighting condition (when it is in sunlight while the observer is in shadow) — conflating two separate factors.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has correctly identified reflected light as the mechanism but incorrectly named the source as the Moon rather than the Sun — showing partial understanding of the reflected-light principle but misidentifying the primary light source.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who select the orbital-pass option can be directed to consider: a satellite passes overhead many times a day — why are only some passes visible? This redirects them from geometry to the lighting condition.

competency.competency_text: Explains celestial phenomena including Moon phases, calendar structure, and artificial satellites by tracing each to the observable periodic motions of the Earth and Moon.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Festival | Calendar basis | Typical Gregorian date behaviour
Diwali | Luni-solar (new Moon of Kartika) | Shifts, but within roughly a month's range
Eid-ul-Fitr | Purely lunar (crescent sighting after Ramazan) | Shifts across different Gregorian months over years
Makar Sankranti | Solar sidereal | Nearly fixed; drifts by about 1 day per 71 years
Buddha Purnima | Luni-solar (full Moon of Vaisakha) | Shifts, but within roughly a month's range
assessment_items.question_text: Refer to the table provided. A student notices that Eid-ul-Fitr shifts across different Gregorian months over a cycle of years, while Diwali — also based on a lunar phase — does not shift as widely. Using the table and your calendar knowledge, explain the difference in their date behaviour.
expected_elements: Eid-ul-Fitr follows a purely lunar calendar — 12 lunar months of approximately 29.5 days give a lunar year of approximately 354 days, about 11 days shorter than the Gregorian solar year; with no correction applied, Eid moves earlier in the Gregorian calendar by approximately 11 days each year, eventually cycling through all Gregorian months.

Diwali follows a luni-solar calendar, which inserts an intercalary month (Adhika Maasa) every two to three years when the accumulated lunar-solar gap approaches a full month; this correction prevents Diwali from drifting more than roughly one month away from its seasonal position.
The key difference is the intercalary correction: luni-solar calendars apply it, purely lunar calendars do not.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who can identify the difference in the table but struggle to explain the mechanism can be prompted: 'What does the luni-solar calendar do every two to three years that the purely lunar calendar does not?' — leading them to the intercalary month. Students who prefer calculation can be asked to show how many years it takes for the 11-day annual drift to cycle Eid through all 12 Gregorian months.

assessment_items.stage_label: Trace each celestial phenomenon to its underlying orbital motion
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can trace each celestial phenomenon studied in the chapter — Moon phases, eclipses, calendar units, festival date patterns, and satellite visibility — to the specific periodic orbital motion of the Earth or Moon responsible for it.

assessment_items.question_text: A student lists four celestial phenomena: (i) the length of a day, (ii) the phases of the Moon, (iii) the solar year, (iv) the lunar eclipse. Which row correctly matches each phenomenon to its primary orbital motion?

options.label: A
options.text: Day — Earth's revolution around the Sun; Moon phases — Moon's rotation on its axis; Solar year — Earth's rotation; Lunar eclipse — Moon's revolution bringing it in front of the Sun.

options.label: B
options.text: Day — Earth's rotation; Moon phases — Earth's shadow falling on the Moon; Solar year — Earth's revolution; Lunar eclipse — Moon passing in front of the Sun.

options.label: C
options.text: Day — Earth's rotation; Moon phases — Moon's revolution around Earth; Solar year — Earth's revolution around the Sun; Lunar eclipse — Moon's revolution bringing it into Earth's shadow at a full Moon alignment.

options.label: D
options.text: Day — Earth's rotation; Moon phases — Moon's revolution around Earth; Solar year — Moon's revolution around Earth multiplied by 12; Lunar eclipse — Moon's revolution bringing it into Earth's shadow.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student has confused which motion produces which unit — swapping Earth's rotation (day) and Earth's revolution (year), and incorrectly attributing Moon phases to the Moon's own axial rotation rather than its revolution around Earth.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student correctly matches day and year to their orbital motions but retains the core misconception that Moon phases are caused by Earth's shadow — the exact confusion the chapter's phase model was designed to resolve.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student correctly matches day, phases, and eclipse but derives the solar year incorrectly from the Moon's orbital period multiplied by 12 — conflating the lunar year calculation with the definition of the solar year.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who select option C (shadow misconception for phases) should be prompted to recall which model they used in the ball-and-torch unit and whether Earth's shadow was involved in producing the phase sequence they observed.

assessment_items.question_text: A designer proposes a new calendar that uses only the Moon's phase cycle to count both months and years — defining the year as exactly 12 lunar months with no corrections. Which of the following is the strongest argument against this proposal, based on the orbital motions covered in this chapter?

options.label: A
options.text: This calendar would drift from the seasons by approximately 11 days each year because Earth's revolution around the Sun (365 days) is not a multiple of the Moon's phase cycle (29.5 days), causing seasons to fall on different months over time.

options.label: B
options.text: This calendar would fail because it does not account for Earth's rotation, which means the length of the day would gradually become misaligned with the calendar date.

options.label: C
options.text: This calendar would fail because the Moon does not actually complete exactly 12 orbits of Earth per solar year, making it impossible to divide the year into 12 equal lunar months.

options.label: D
options.text: This calendar would fail because the Moon's orbital period changes each year due to Earth's varying distance from the Sun, making the phase cycle unreliable as a unit of time.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student has confused a true astronomical fact (the Moon does not complete exactly 12 orbits per solar year) with the argument presented in the chapter, which frames the problem as a drift of approximately 11 days per year rather than as an impossibility of equal division.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student introduces a false premise — that the Moon's orbital period changes due to Earth's distance from the Sun — which is not presented in the chapter; this indicates recall of an external but incorrect notion rather than chapter-based reasoning.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student conflates two separate calendar problems: the lunar-solar drift (the relevant objection) and the day-count alignment issue, which is a separate concern about the solar day and is already handled independently in any calendar system.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who select option B (close but not quite the right framing) can be pushed further: 'The Moon does orbit approximately 12.4 times per year — is the problem that it's not exactly 12, or is the problem something that accumulates over many years?' This redirects them from the fractional cycle to the 11-day annual shortfall.

assessment_items.question_text: The Indian National Calendar was established in 1956 following the recommendation of the Calendar Reform Committee chaired by astrophysicist Meghnad Saha. It is a solar calendar whose year begins the day after the spring equinox and whose month names are drawn from traditional Indian luni-solar calendars. Explain why a solar calendar was chosen over a purely lunar or luni-solar calendar for official national use, and identify the orbital motion or astronomical event on which the Indian National Calendar's year is anchored.
look_for: Response explains that a solar calendar keeps its months in alignment with the seasons year after year — important for agriculture and civil administration — whereas a purely lunar calendar drifts by approximately 11 days per year.

Response notes that the spring equinox — which marks Earth reaching a specific position in its orbit around the Sun — is used to anchor the start of the year, grounding the calendar in Earth's revolution.

Response distinguishes this from a luni-solar calendar: while luni-solar calendars also broadly track the seasons (through the intercalary month), their month boundaries still follow the Moon's phase cycle, making them less precise for uniform national administrative use.

Strong responses may also mention that the Gregorian calendar is also solar and uses the tropical year (time between successive spring equinoxes), connecting the Indian National Calendar to the same astronomical basis.

ECR.inclusivity: Students who can identify the spring equinox as the anchor but struggle to explain the season-alignment rationale can be asked: 'If you were a farmer deciding when to plant, which would be more reliable — a date that always falls in the same season, or one that drifts by 11 days each year?' Students who know the calendar reform context may include the role of Meghnad Saha; this adds historical depth but is not required for a complete response.

OPEN_TASK.format_type: Classification or sorting task with justification
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The final stage implied LO requires students to trace multiple distinct celestial phenomena to their specific orbital motions simultaneously — a classification-with-causal-justification task is the most direct demonstration vehicle for this multi-phenomenon tracing operation.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: A complete response demonstrates that the student can identify the correct orbital motion for each phenomenon, link it to an observable physical effect, and extend that link to a real calendar or practical consequence — the full causal chain the dissolution test names.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The three-column structure ensures students must supply three distinct cognitive moves for each phenomenon: causal identification, observational evidence, and consequence — a weak response stops at naming the motion without articulating the chain. The five phenomena are chosen to sample all major topics in the chapter: phases, eclipses, lunar calendar drift, satellite visibility, and solar calendar correction.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong responses name a specific orbital motion for each row (not just 'the Moon moves'), provide an observable or measurable link (e.g. the Moon's angular separation from the Sun decreases as the waning phase progresses), and articulate a specific consequence (e.g. Eid drifts across Gregorian months because no intercalary correction is applied). Weak responses name the phenomenon twice or state the consequence as a repetition of the observable effect without identifying the orbital cause.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find the eclipse row most challenging can be directed to re-examine why a lunar eclipse requires a specific alignment (Earth between Sun and Moon) that the Moon's tilted orbit prevents in most months. Students who complete all five rows accurately can be asked to add a sixth row of their own invention — choosing any other phenomenon from the chapter and completing the three columns.
